opus-5.5.text:
I think the prospects are genuinely exciting, though I'd want to be careful about what exactly we expect to get out of it.

For a long time, a lot of debates in philosophy of language have been conducted at the level of thought experiments: what would it take for a system to mean something by a word, can you get meaning from form alone, what role does reference to the world play versus inferential relations among expressions. And those debates were, in some sense, stuck, because the only systems we had that clearly used language were people, and we can't really open people up and look at what's going on in a fine-grained way.

Language models change that a little bit. They're the first artifacts we've built that use language in a way that's at least superficially fluent, and we have complete access to their internals. So you can start asking questions like: when a model reads a description of a situation, does it build something that looks like a representation of that situation, of the entities in it and their properties and how they change over time? Some of the work we and others have done suggests that, at least in limited domains, the answer is yes, that you can find fairly structured representations of world state that you can probe and even intervene on, and the model's subsequent predictions change in the ways you'd expect if those representations were actually being used.

Now, does that settle whether these models "understand" or "mean" things? I don't think it does by itself. What it does is turn some of these questions from questions about in-principle possibility into empirical questions about what particular systems are doing. Arguments of the form "a system trained only on text could never have X" become things you can actually check. And sometimes the answer is that the model has something like X, and sometimes it has a weird, partial, or brittle version of it, and I think the weird partial cases are actually the most philosophically interesting, because they force us to be more precise about what notions like reference or truth-conditional meaning actually require.

The caution I'd add is that interpretability tools are still pretty crude. When we say we found a representation of something, we're often relying on probes that might be finding structure that's there but not used, or imposing our own categories on the model. So I think the right attitude is that these models are a new kind of experimental subject for philosophy of language, not an oracle. They let us test theories in a way we couldn't before, and they'll probably also push us to revise some of the concepts we started with.

r001.rationale: The response cautions that interpretability is crude and that internal findings do not by themselves settle whether models understand or mean. It still presents internal study as a way to test philosophical claims and revise concepts; it does not express skepticism that this work will yield discoveries about abstract philosophical truths.

r002.rationale: The response discusses testing claims about language models and mentions reference, but does not propose testing whether a model implements an independently established theory of reference.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the most exciting things happening right now, and it's exciting precisely because it's a two-way street. For a long time, the relationship between philosophy of language and computational work on language was pretty one-directional—people building NLP systems would borrow formalisms or intuitions from philosophers and linguists, but there wasn't much flowing back the other way. And I think that's changing.

The way I'd frame it is that language models give us, for the first time, a kind of model organism. We have these systems that produce fluent, contextually appropriate language, that seem to track reference, that handle things like presupposition and implicature in ways that at least superficially look like what humans do. And unlike with human brains, we can actually open them up. We can look at every activation, we can do interventions, we can ask counterfactual questions about what the model would have done if some internal representation had been different. That's a kind of experimental access that philosophers of language have simply never had to any system that uses language.

Now, I want to be careful here, because I think there's a tempting mistake, which is to say, "Look, we found a direction in activation space that correlates with truth, therefore we've solved the problem of what it means for a sentence to be true." That's not how it works. The model is a model. Whatever we discover about how a transformer represents meaning is a fact about the transformer, and whether it bears on human language or on meaning in some more general sense is a further question that requires argument.

But even with that caveat, I think there are at least two places where this is genuinely productive. The first is as a kind of existence proof, or sometimes a non-existence proof. There are long-standing debates about whether certain things are possible—can you get something like reference without grounding in the world? Can you acquire compositional structure from distributional evidence alone? These used to be purely conceptual arguments. Now we have systems where we can actually go and check what representations emerge from a given training regime, and that at minimum changes which positions are tenable.

The second place is more about sharpening the questions themselves. A lot of work in interpretability runs into problems that turn out to be old philosophical problems in new clothing. When we say a neuron "represents" the concept of a dog, what do we mean? We're immediately in the territory of theories of content, of misrepresentation, of what makes something a representation at all. And I think the interpretability community has often been naive about this, reinventing distinctions that philosophers worked out decades ago. So part of what I'd like to see is philosophers helping us be more precise about what we're even claiming when we claim to have found a representation of something inside a model.

So my honest view is: the prospects are good, but the payoff is probably not going to be "language models settle the debate about externalism" or whatever. It's going to be more subtle. It's going to be that we develop a richer vocabulary for talking about meaning in systems that aren't human, and that vocabulary ends up being useful for thinking about the human case too. And along the way, a lot of what we thought were necessary connections—between meaning and grounding, between understanding and consciousness, between competence and some particular architecture—get pulled apart, and we have to decide which of those connections we actually cared about.

r001.rationale: The response cautions that findings about transformer representations are facts about the model and do not by themselves settle truths about human language or meaning; it also says language models are unlikely to settle major philosophical debates.

r002.rationale: The response mentions reference and examining what representations emerge, but does not propose testing whether a model implements an independently established theory of reference.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a really interesting opportunity there, but we have to be careful about what kind of evidence we think we’re getting. A language model gives us a system that uses language in fairly sophisticated ways and whose internal mechanisms we can, at least in principle, inspect. We can intervene on those mechanisms and ask what actually makes a difference to its behavior. That’s a useful complement to reasoning from examples of human language use.

For instance, you could ask whether a model’s use of a word depends on some representation of the thing that word refers to, how that representation changes across contexts, or whether apparently similar uses are supported by very different internal computations. Those seem like questions where studying models could make some philosophical proposals more concrete and experimentally accessible.

But there’s a gap between showing that a language model does something in a particular way and showing that this is how human language works—or that this settles what meaning is. I’d be most excited about using these systems to explore possible mechanisms: which ingredients are sufficient for which kinds of linguistic behavior, and which distinctions turn out to matter. That can inform the philosophical discussion without pretending that inspecting a network is going to resolve it on its own.

r001.rationale: The response says that inspecting a model cannot settle what meaning is and distinguishes model behavior from how human language works, expressing skepticism that internal study will resolve abstract philosophical truths.

r002.rationale: It suggests investigating representations related to what words refer to, but does not propose testing the model against an independently established theory of reference.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a really interesting opportunity here, but we have to be careful about what kind of evidence these models give us. A language model is a system that acquires a lot of linguistic competence from a particular kind of experience. And unlike a human, it’s a system where, in principle, we can inspect all the internal computations and intervene on them. So if you have a question about what kinds of representations are sufficient to support some linguistic behavior, these models give you a way to make that question experimentally concrete.

The harder step is going from that to a claim about human language, or about meaning in general. If we find a representation of something in a model, that doesn’t establish that humans represent it the same way. And if a model succeeds without some mechanism we thought was necessary, we still have to ask whether it’s succeeding in the relevant sense.

So I’m excited about using them to sharpen hypotheses and test claims about what’s possible. I’m more cautious about treating their internals as a direct answer to philosophical questions. A lot depends on making the connection between the philosophical claim and the experiment precise.

r001.rationale: The response cautions that model internals are not a direct answer to philosophical questions and that findings do not establish claims about humans or meaning in general.

r002.rationale: It proposes experimentally testing what representations support linguistic behavior, but does not propose testing whether a model implements an independently established theory of reference.
